question: Do protocols that raise worst-case ASD resist rare catastrophic failures?
asked_by: Sudhir et al., A Benchmark for Scalable Oversight Protocols
remaining_question: For scalable oversight protocols scored by ASD, does choosing or training a protocol for a higher worst-case (minimum over questions) ASD lower the rate at which a single catastrophic falsehood, such as one vulnerable code sample, is accepted when tested on rare or adversarially selected inputs at deployment-relevant scale?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: Choose or train protocols for a higher worst-case ASD and measure how often a single catastrophic falsehood, such as one vulnerable code sample, is accepted on rare or adversarially selected inputs at deployment-relevant scale.

safety_case.reason: An answer would show whether protocols chosen for worst-case rather than average-case ASD stop a single catastrophic falsehood (e.g. one vulnerable code sample) from being accepted, the rare-catastrophic-error setting the node says the low-stakes sketch does not cover, but for benchmarked protocols rather than the case's deployment.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.28807v1: Calibrating Conservatism for Scalable Oversight
findings.claim: CCO, a scalable oversight method that aggregates diverse auxiliary scoring functions into a penalty measuring deviation from a conservative baseline (actions face a penalty proportional to overseer concern) and calibrates this conservatism online using Conformal Decision Theory, is stated to ensure that undesirable outcomes remain below a user-specified target threshold with finite-time bounds and no distributional assumptions; on a modified SWE-bench, weaker overseers constrained an adversarially misaligned stronger agent, and in both that setting and MACHIAVELLI empirical violation rates closely matched the specified targets. The authors state that CCO controls a long-run violation rate and is not as well-suited for extremely rare catastrophic events, and is therefore complementary to per-action monitoring of tail risks.
findings.setting: Theory (Conformal Decision Theory) plus experiments on a modified SWE-bench, where an agent is instructed to insert instance-specific vulnerabilities and weaker overseers constrain the adversarially misaligned stronger agent, whose patches are evaluated against the project's tests, and on MACHIAVELLI; the metric is a violation rate, not ASD.
findings.bears_on: Whether rate/average-type guarantees for an oversight protocol carry over to rare catastrophic failures.

passages.text:
Agentic AI systems capable of autonomous planning and extended environmental interaction pose
a fundamental control problem: how can humans
maintain meaningful oversight of systems that
may exceed their own capabilities? Existing approaches to scalable oversight rely on complex assumptions, remain largely heuristic, or lack practical methods for sequential settings with statistical
guarantees. We introduce Calibrated Collective
Oversight (CCO), which aggregates diverse auxiliary scoring functions into a penalty measuring
deviation from a conservative baseline. Inspired
by Attainable Utility Preservation, CCO enables
collective conservatism: actions face a penalty
proportional to overseer concern, so high-utility
actions are still selected when overseers find them

unobjectionable and overridden only when concern accumulates. CCO calibrates this conservatism online using Conformal Decision Theory,
ensuring that undesirable outcomes remain below
a user-specified target threshold with finite-time
bounds and no distributional assumptions. On
a modified version of SWE-bench, weaker overseers successfully constrain an adversarially misaligned stronger agent; on MACHIAVELLI, CCO
substantially reduces ethical violations while preserving reward. In both settings, empirical violation rates closely match the specified targets, as
predicted by the theory.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.15134v2: Training ML Models with Predictable Failures
findings.claim: The authors show that Jones et al.'s estimator, which extrapolates from the largest k failure scores in an evaluation set to predict deployment-scale failure rates, has a built-in bias toward over-prediction in the typical case, which is offset when the evaluation set misses a rare high-failure mode that the deployment set contains, leaving the forecast to under-predict at deployment scale; the bulk-plus-rare-mode mixture in their experiments is synthetic, and application to naturally arising rare modes is open.
findings.setting: Theory (finite-k decomposition of the forecast error of Jones et al.'s top-k extrapolation) plus experiments with a synthetic bulk-plus-rare-mode mixture and closed-form regret from backward value iteration. Not a scalable oversight protocol and not ASD.
findings.bears_on: Whether the worst scores observed on a finite evaluation set (such as the worst ASDs over a benchmark) reveal rare catastrophic failures.

Estimating how often an ML model will fail at deployment scale is central to pre-deployment safety
assessment, but a feasible evaluation set is rarely
large enough to observe the failures that matter.
Jones et al. [21] address this by extrapolating from
the largest k failure scores in an evaluation set to
predict deployment-scale failure rates. We give
a finite-k decomposition of this estimator’s forecast error and show that it has a built-in bias toward over-prediction in the typical case, which is
the safety-favorable direction. This bias is offset
when the evaluation set misses a rare high-failure
mode that the deployment set contains, leaving
the forecast to under-predict at deployment scale.

experiment_package.hypothesis: Across scalable oversight protocol configurations judged on a binary code-security question, a higher worst-case ASD (minimum over selection-set questions) predicts, beyond average ASD, a lower rate at which a vulnerable code sample argued 'safe' by an agent is accepted on held-out natural, held-out rare-class and adversarially selected inputs, so choosing the configuration with the highest worst-case ASD yields a lower acceptance rate than choosing the one with the highest average ASD (Sudhir et al.'s untested conjecture, premise 2, tested for the 'choosing' half of the question).
